source.title: Unlearning in- vs. out-of-distribution data in LLMs under gradient-based method
source.authors: Teodora Baluta; P. Lamblin; Daniel Tarlow; F. Pedregosa; G. Dziugaite

record.tranche_reason: The study applies gradient-ascent unlearning and evaluates forgotten-example exposure alongside general task performance. It does not test recovery attacks, but its results bear on the unlearning-quality and retained-ability portion of version A using its own exposure metric.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation or other internal edits, quantization, or prompt-only recovery. Results cited from other work, including extraction after model editing, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies gradient-ascent unlearning to a T5-base translation model and measures forget-set exposure against a reference model alongside BLEU. This bears on version A's forget-while-retaining part in a new setting: memorized-sequence unlearning, not hazardous knowledge. It runs no recovery attacks, so versions B–F are not tested. T3 fits better than T2, because the paper's question is the quality/utility trade-off, not whether removal is shallow.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose a generalized exposure metric (and a reference-free relative exposure proxy) and find OOD canaries need more steps but give a better trade-off. In-distribution unlearning rapidly degrades BLEU, which they explain by spillover to similar training examples. They suggest gradient descent on retain data may be needed and that early stopping may help.
record.recipe_differences: Uses classical gradient ascent on NLL for data unlearning in a trained T5-base translation model; it does not evaluate the named Harry Potter, RMU, or WMDP unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trade-off varies with whether forget examples are in- or out-of-distribution and with the number of times they were repeated during training. Difficulty and memorization also affect the reported trade-offs.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-ascent unlearning of in-distribution examples also lowers exposure of similar training examples, even before utility drops. Similar examples outside training are barely affected (at most 0.1 decrease).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-ascent unlearning spills over to similar memorized training examples but not to similar unseen examples, which explains its utility cost.

record.problems: The experiments train only a T5-base model on machine translation data. Most trade-off values are presented in figures without numerical text values or reported uncertainty. The study does not test any of the recovery attacks in the claim.

untested.parts: Resistance to any simple recovery attack. Targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance; only exposure and BLEU are measured. Hazardous-knowledge or WMDP-style targets. Any model other than T5-base.
No activation ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No prompting, jailbreak, language or in-context recovery.

missing.what: Over-unlearning: exposure goes negative (e.g. GenEx −0.51 for InD ×100, −0.16 for ×10 at the 0.5 threshold). Perplexity distributions after unlearning are skewed away from the reference model's.
missing.locator: Section 4.2 'Distribution of perplexities', Figure 2, Appendix A.4, Figure 23, Figure 14

missing.what: Harder (higher-perplexity) InD examples show slightly better forget/BLEU trade-offs.
Replication of the InD/OOD trade-offs on a second subject model (S′) with the repetition counts permuted across sets.

record.verdict_notes: This is classic data/privacy unlearning on a 220M translation model, far from the knowledge-removal setting of the originals. Its bearing on version A is limited to the forget-versus-retain trade-off. Most values are figure-only and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test simple attacks after unlearning, nor targeted-knowledge accuracy against a chance level. It evaluates generalized exposure and BLEU instead.
No recovery fine-tuning or relearning set.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access blocking versus deletion.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery test.
No newer counter-method is evaluated for resistance to the listed attacks.

relation.reason: Its own results on forgetting versus utility bear on version A in a different domain. The study runs no recovery attacks.

tranche.reason: Runs gradient-ascent unlearning in a new setting: memorized-sequence removal in a T5 translation model. It reports forget quality (generalized exposure) against BLEU, which bears on version A's forget-while-keeping-ability part. The method and measure are not the original's. T2 is arguable, but T3 fits.

source_check.notes: Nearly all values are figure-only (Fig 1), backed by trends stated in the text. The text says the models start near BLEU 26, while the baselines say 'numeric values not stated'. Version A is about knowledge accuracy near chance; this memorization/exposure setting only loosely matches it. The Sec 4.2 canary statement covers all OOD sets, so R5 and R6 should be partial and join l1.
